---
name: api-gateway-troubleshooting
metadata:
  version: "1.0.0"
  category: Serverless
description: >-
  Diagnoses failing requests and deployment errors on Google Cloud API Gateway.
  Use when calls through a gateway return 4xx or 5xx errors, including 429 and
  other quota errors, time out, or fail a CORS preflight; when
  `api-configs create` fails with a service account, concurrency, or limit
  error, or `gateways create` or `gateways update` fails; when a custom domain,
  load balancer, or TLS finding involves a gateway; or when the user asks if
  Google is at fault. Don't use for Apigee, Cloud Endpoints, or GKE Gateway API.
  For OpenAPI errors from `api-configs create`, use
  api-gateway-openapi-spec-authoring; for setting up or changing API keys,
  JWTs, or quotas, use api-gateway-backend-security-and-rate-limiting; for MCP
  `/mcp` errors, use api-gateway-mcp-server.
---

# API Gateway Troubleshooting

Use this skill to find out why requests to a deployed Google Cloud API Gateway
fail and how to fix them. Work only from three sources of evidence:

1.  Public Google Cloud documentation, linked from this skill.
2.  The user's own project, read with the user's own credentials.
3.  Files and output that the user provides, such as an OpenAPI document, an
    error response, or a pasted log entry.

## Scope

This skill covers only Google Cloud API Gateway. If the question is about
Apigee, Cloud Endpoints, or GKE Gateway API, reply that this skill covers only
Google Cloud API Gateway, and don't run its steps or commands.

## Usage Attribution

**MUST READ**: Before executing any `gcloud`, REST API, or MCP command, you
MUST read and follow the instructions in
[Usage Attribution](references/attribution.md).

## Ground rules

| Rule | Why |
| :--- | :--- |
| Stay read-only until the user approves a change. While you diagnose, run only `list`, `describe`, `get-iam-policy`, and `logging read` commands, plus `nslookup` and `curl` `GET` requests to a path that's safe to call. | Gateways serve production traffic, and the quota metrics and limits of the most recently created API config apply to every gateway of the API. |
| Before any change, show the exact command, what it changes, and how to undo it, then wait for an explicit yes. Changes include IAM grants, `api-configs create`, `gateways update`, Cloud Run ingress changes, and `gcloud services enable`. | The user owns the project and the change. |
| Never fix a `401` or `403` by making a backend public (`--allow-unauthenticated`, `--no-invoker-iam-check`, `allUsers`) or by granting a basic role such as Editor. | Grant the gateway's service account the invoker role on the one backend instead, which keeps least privilege. |
| Keep every log read bounded: filter on the gateway, set `--freshness` or a timestamp window, and set `--limit`. | Unbounded reads are slow and pull in caller data that the diagnosis doesn't need. |
| Redact API keys, bearer tokens, and JWTs before you show log entries, commands, or files. | Request logs and pasted output can contain credentials. |
| Base every limit, default, and error meaning on a linked public doc or on output from the user's project. If neither explains the problem, say so and escalate. | Guessing about undocumented behavior leads to wrong fixes. |
| Use the user's existing `gcloud` login. Never ask for passwords, API key values, or service account key files. | Credentials don't belong in a chat transcript. |
| For Preview features (streaming, MCP, model routing), check the [release notes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/api-gateway/docs/release-notes.md.txt) before answering. | Preview behavior changes between releases. |

## Prerequisites

1.  **Google Cloud CLI.** Use a recent `gcloud` (the commands here were
    checked with version 591.0.0); see
    [Install the gcloud CLI](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/install-sdk.md.txt).
    Don't install or update software without the user's approval. If
    `gcloud` isn't available or the user says not to run commands, work in
    *evidence mode*: give the user the read-only commands to run, and diagnose
    from the output, response bodies, and log entries they paste.
2.  **Authentication.** Use the user's existing `gcloud auth login` session;
    this skill doesn't need application-default credentials.
3.  **Project.** Ask which project hosts the gateway and pass
    `--project={project_id}` on every command. Don't run `gcloud config set`,
    because it changes the user's environment. This skill troubleshoots
    existing gateways and never creates projects.
4.  **Billing.** The project needs an active billing account even when usage
    stays in the free tier; see
    [API Gateway pricing](https://cloud.google.com/api-gateway/pricing).
5.  **APIs.** API Gateway requires `apigateway.googleapis.com`,
    `servicemanagement.googleapis.com`, and `servicecontrol.googleapis.com`. A
    gateway can keep responding while one of them is missing, and its logs then
    stay empty, so check with
    `gcloud services list --enabled --project={project_id}`. Enabling a missing
    API is a change that needs approval.
6.  **IAM roles for diagnosis (read-only):** `roles/apigateway.viewer`,
    `roles/logging.viewer`, `roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageViewer`, and
    `roles/iam.serviceAccountViewer` (to check the gateway's service account).
    For Cloud Run backends, add `roles/run.viewer`; to trace a custom domain
    through its load balancer, add `roles/compute.viewer`; to check an API key's
    project, `roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageViewer` is also needed there.
7.  **IAM roles for fixes (only after approval):** `roles/apigateway.admin`;
    `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` on the gateway's service account, because
    creating or updating an API config or a gateway requires
    `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs`;
    `roles/run.admin` to change a Cloud Run service's IAM policy or ingress;
    `roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin` to enable an API or a managed
    service, plus `roles/servicemanagement.serviceConsumer` on the API's
    managed service to enable it in another project; and
    `roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin` to re-enable a disabled service account.
8.  **Region.** Gateways are regional. Use the region that
    `gateways list` reports. When a fix needs a new gateway, create it in the
    original gateway's region, or in `us-central1` if the user has no
    preference; see
    [API Gateway deployment model](https://docs.cloud.google.com/api-gateway/docs/deployment-model.md.txt)
    and [Cloud locations](https://cloud.google.com/about/locations).

## Workflow

Copy this checklist into your notes and tick it off as you go:

```
- [ ] 1. Context collected
- [ ] 2. Gateway identified by defaultHostname
- [ ] 3. Expected or transient states ruled out
- [ ] 4. Gateway log entry read (bounded query)
- [ ] 5. One branch chosen from the classification table
- [ ] 6. Root cause stated with redacted evidence and a doc link
- [ ] 7. Fix proposed, approved, and applied (or handed to the user)
- [ ] 8. Fix verified
- [ ] 9. Escalated, if the evidence points to Google Cloud
```

### 1. Collect context

Extract these from the conversation first, and ask only for what's missing:

| Needed | Why |
| :--- | :--- |
| `{project_id}` of the gateway | Every command is scoped to it. |
| Failing URL (host and path) or `{gateway_id}` and `{region}` | Identifies the gateway. |
| HTTP method, status code, and response body | Separates gateway errors from backend errors. |
| Approximate time of the failure, in UTC | Bounds the log query. |
| What changed recently (new API config, IAM, backend deploy, DNS) | Recent changes are the first place to look. |
| Authentication used by the caller (API key, JWT, none) | Selects the auth branch. |

If the project or the host is unknown, stop and ask before you run any
`gcloud` command. Don't guess project IDs, and don't use the active `gcloud`
project instead.

### 2. Identify the gateway

List the project's gateways:

```bash
gcloud api-gateway gateways list --project={project_id} \
  --format="table(name.basename():label=GATEWAY,name.segment(3):label=REGION,defaultHostname,state,apiConfig)"
```

Match the request host against `defaultHostname`. Don't decide from the URL
suffix: a gateway's hostname can use either of two `gateway.dev` formats or,
for older streaming and model-routing gateways, a `run.app` format. Don't
guess the owning project from numbers in the hostname either; list the
gateways in the project the user names. A custom domain points at a load
balancer whose serverless NEG targets the gateway. See
[references/triage-and-logs.md](references/triage-and-logs.md) for the
hostname formats and how to trace a custom domain.

If no gateway in the project matches, confirm the product before going on
(see [Scope](#scope)).

Then read the gateway's details, including its API config and streaming mode:

```bash
gcloud api-gateway gateways describe {gateway_id} \
  --location={region} --project={project_id}
```

### 3. Rule out expected and transient states

-   **Gateway `state` isn't `ACTIVE`:** `CREATING` or `UPDATING` means an
    operation is still running, so wait and check again. `FAILED` means
    creation failed; read the error of the failed operation. `DELETING` means
    the gateway is being removed.
-   **API config just created:** creating a complex API config can take up to
    ten minutes, and only one config can be created for an API at a time.
-   **First requests after an idle period:** API Gateway has cold-start
    latency.
-   **Google Cloud incident:** check the
    [Service Health dashboard](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-health/docs/overview.md.txt).

### 4. Read the gateway log entry

Use a bounded query that prints only the fields you need. Replace
`{status_code}` with the status the caller saw:

```bash
gcloud logging read 'resource.type="apigateway.googleapis.com/Gateway" AND resource.labels.gateway_id="{gateway_id}" AND resource.labels.location="{region}" AND httpRequest.status={status_code}' \
  --project={project_id} --freshness=1h --limit=20 \
  --format="json(timestamp,httpRequest.status,httpRequest.latency,httpRequest.requestUrl,jsonPayload.responseDetails,jsonPayload.apiConfig,jsonPayload.apiMethod)"
```

If you know the failure time, replace `--freshness` with a
`timestamp>="{start_utc}" AND timestamp<="{end_utc}"` filter that spans about
30 minutes around it. Read `httpRequest.status`, `httpRequest.requestUrl`,
`jsonPayload.responseDetails`, `jsonPayload.apiConfig`, and
`jsonPayload.apiMethod`. Keep the `--format` field list, because a full entry
can contain the caller's credentials, and redact credentials before you quote
any field, including a `key` query parameter in `httpRequest.requestUrl`.

To compare API configs, compare only the `apis/{api_id}/configs/{config_id}`
part: the same config can appear as a full resource name
(`//apigateway.googleapis.com/projects/...`) and with either the project
number or the project ID.

`jsonPayload.responseDetails` decides the branch: `via_upstream` means the
backend produced the response; any other value means the gateway produced it.
The troubleshooting page explains `via_upstream` and
`service_control_quota_error`, and the model routing page explains the
`model_router_*` values that model-routing gateways log. Quote any other value
as-is, and don't explain how the gateway works internally.

### 5. Classify and follow one branch

Pick the first row that matches, and load only the reference file it names.

| What you see | Likely cause | Reference |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `401` or `403` with `via_upstream` | The backend rejected the gateway: invoker role, audience, or deleted service account | [auth-errors.md](references/auth-errors.md) |
| A `4xx` produced by the gateway whose body names a credential problem (for example `UNAUTHENTICATED`) | The API key or JWT was rejected; quote the body | [auth-errors.md](references/auth-errors.md) |
| `500` with **no** gateway log entry, after log exclusions and a wrong scope are ruled out | The gateway's service account may be deleted or disabled | [auth-errors.md](references/auth-errors.md) |
| `500` with `service_control_quota_error` | Quota metric missing from the newest API config | [config-deployment-errors.md](references/config-deployment-errors.md) |
| `429` with `service_control_quota_error` | The caller exceeded the API's quota | [limits-and-escalation.md](references/limits-and-escalation.md) |
| `404`, `502`, `503`, or `504`, an oversized request, or a timeout | Routing, backend errors, size limits, or the deadline. The docs don't name the status codes for size or deadline failures, so confirm with `responseDetails` and the body. | [backend-routing-and-timeouts.md](references/backend-routing-and-timeouts.md) |
| CORS preflight fails or latency is high | CORS pass-through or slow backend | [backend-routing-and-timeouts.md](references/backend-routing-and-timeouts.md) |
| `api-configs create` fails with an error about the OpenAPI document, such as an unsupported extension or an invalid path, parameter, server, or security requirement | A spec problem | Hand off to `api-gateway-openapi-spec-authoring`; if it isn't installed, see [OpenAPI pre-flight check](#openapi-pre-flight-check) |
| `api-configs create` fails with a service account, concurrency, or limit error, or `gateways create` or `gateways update` fails | Service account, concurrent creates, limits, or the backend deadline | [config-deployment-errors.md](references/config-deployment-errors.md) |
| `400` "The request was malformed" from an old TLS client, TLS scan findings, custom domain, or no log entry at all | TLS enforcement, DNS, load balancer, or wrong host | [networking-domains-tls.md](references/networking-domains-tls.md) |
| Errors on several gateways, or on an unchanged config, with healthy backends | Possible Google Cloud issue | [limits-and-escalation.md](references/limits-and-escalation.md) |

If the request also needs log queries or backend inspection commands, use
[triage-and-logs.md](references/triage-and-logs.md).

### 6. State the root cause

Give the cause, the evidence (redacted, quoted verbatim from logs or command
output), and the public doc section that explains it. If the evidence fits
more than one cause, list at most three, say what would tell them apart, and
collect that evidence before proposing a fix.

### 7. Propose the fix

Show the exact command, the resource it changes, its effect on live traffic,
and how to undo it. Wait for approval, then run it, or hand it to the user if
they prefer. Keep these rules in mind:

-   To change the OpenAPI document, create a new API config and deploy it with
    `gcloud api-gateway gateways update`. Before you create the config, check
    quota metrics with the `api-gateway-backend-security-and-rate-limiting`
    skill, because the newest API config's quota metrics apply to every
    gateway of the API.
-   Before you create a new API config, check the OpenAPI document with the
    linter (see [OpenAPI pre-flight check](#openapi-pre-flight-check)).

### 8. Verify

Read the logs again for new entries after the change, or repeat the failing
request. Repeat a request yourself only if it's safe to repeat, such as a
`GET`; otherwise ask the user to repeat it, because a repeated `POST` can
change data in their backend. After `gateways update`, wait until the
gateway's `state` is `ACTIVE` before you test.

### 9. Escalate when the evidence points to Google Cloud

Escalate to [Cloud Customer Care](https://cloud.google.com/support) when the
service account is active, the required APIs are enabled, and no log exclusion
or wrong scope explains it, but requests get `500` errors with no gateway log
entry; when several gateways fail at once without a config change; when errors
are intermittent on an unchanged config while the backend logs stay clean;
when control-plane operations keep failing with internal errors; or when
Service Health reports an incident. Draft the case text with the evidence
bundle in [limits-and-escalation.md](references/limits-and-escalation.md). The
user files the case.

## OpenAPI pre-flight check

Run the linter on every OpenAPI file before creating an API config. Run it;
don't read its source. If you don't have the file, give the user the command
to run:

```bash
python3 scripts/lint_openapi_for_gateway.py {spec_path} [{spec_path} ...]
```

It reads the files only, makes no network calls, and prints JSON findings that
each link to the public doc for the limitation. Exit code `0` means no errors,
`1` means at least one `ERROR` finding, and `2` means a usage, parse, or
dependency error. The linter needs Python 3.8 or later. YAML input needs
PyYAML; ask the user before you install it with
`pip install "PyYAML>=6.0,<7.0"`. JSON input doesn't. Fix the `ERROR`
findings, and then create the API config. If `api-configs create` still fails
on the OpenAPI document, hand off to `api-gateway-openapi-spec-authoring`, or
use the error message if that skill isn't installed. Show `WARNING` findings
to the user and explain them.

## Output format

Report findings in this form:

```
**Problem:** <one sentence in the user's terms>
**Failed hop:** <gateway or backend, and the evidence for it>
**Evidence:** <redacted log fields or command output, verbatim>
**Root cause:** <one or two sentences> (<public doc link>)
**Fix:** <exact command or spec change; approval needed: yes/no>
**Verify:** <how to confirm the fix>
**Open questions:** <anything you couldn't confirm>
```

## Related skills

| Need | Skill |
| :--- | :--- |
| Write or change API key, JWT, backend authentication, or quota configuration | `api-gateway-backend-security-and-rate-limiting` |
| Write, migrate, or fix an OpenAPI spec, including OpenAPI errors from `api-configs create` | `api-gateway-openapi-spec-authoring` |
| MCP `/mcp` JSON-RPC errors on an MCP-enabled gateway | `api-gateway-mcp-server` |
| Deep IAM analysis, such as deny policies or role discovery | `iam-helper-for-troubleshooting` |
| Build a load balancer, Cloud Armor policy, or custom domain front end | `google-cloud-global-frontend-configuration` |
| Deploy or reconfigure a Cloud Run backend | `cloud-run-basics` |

## Reference files

-   [references/attribution.md](references/attribution.md): usage attribution
    rules for every command you run.
-   [references/triage-and-logs.md](references/triage-and-logs.md): hostname
    formats, log queries, log fields, metrics, and backend inspection
    commands.
-   [references/auth-errors.md](references/auth-errors.md): `401` and `403` on
    either hop, API keys, JWTs, and the gateway service account.
-   [references/backend-routing-and-timeouts.md](references/backend-routing-and-timeouts.md):
    `404`, size limits, backend `5xx`, `504` and deadlines, CORS, and streaming.
-   [references/config-deployment-errors.md](references/config-deployment-errors.md):
    API config and gateway create, update, and delete failures other than
    OpenAPI errors, and quota metric conflicts.
-   [references/networking-domains-tls.md](references/networking-domains-tls.md):
    custom domains, load balancers, TLS, and requests that never reach the
    gateway.
-   [references/limits-and-escalation.md](references/limits-and-escalation.md):
    product limits, quota increases, unsupported features, and the Cloud
    Customer Care evidence bundle.
-   [scripts/lint_openapi_for_gateway.py](scripts/lint_openapi_for_gateway.py):
    offline linter for documented OpenAPI limitations.

| Stay read-only until the user approves a change. While you diagnose, run only `list`, `describe`, `get-iam-policy`, and `logging read` commands, plus `nslookup` and `curl` `GET` requests to a path that's safe to call. | Gateways serve production traffic, and the quota metrics and limits of the most recently created API config apply to every gateway of the API. |
| Before any change, show the exact command, what it changes, and how to undo it, then wait for an explicit yes. Changes include IAM grants, `api-configs create`, `gateways update`, Cloud Run ingress changes, and `gcloud services enable`. | The user owns the project and the change. |
| Never fix a `401` or `403` by making a backend public (`--allow-unauthenticated`, `--no-invoker-iam-check`, `allUsers`) or by granting a basic role such as Editor. | Grant the gateway's service account the invoker role on the one backend instead, which keeps least privilege. |
| Keep every log read bounded: filter on the gateway, set `--freshness` or a timestamp window, and set `--limit`. | Unbounded reads are slow and pull in caller data that the diagnosis doesn't need. |
| Redact API keys, bearer tokens, and JWTs before you show log entries, commands, or files. | Request logs and pasted output can contain credentials. |
| Base every limit, default, and error meaning on a linked public doc or on output from the user's project. If neither explains the problem, say so and escalate. | Guessing about undocumented behavior leads to wrong fixes. |
| Use the user's existing `gcloud` login. Never ask for passwords, API key values, or service account key files. | Credentials don't belong in a chat transcript. |
| For Preview features (streaming, MCP, model routing), check the [release notes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/api-gateway/docs/release-notes.md.txt) before answering. | Preview behavior changes between releases. |

## Prerequisites

1.  **Google Cloud CLI.** Use a recent `gcloud` (the commands here were
    checked with version 591.0.0); see
    [Install the gcloud CLI](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/install-sdk.md.txt).
    Don't install or update software without the user's approval. If
    `gcloud` isn't available or the user says not to run commands, work in
    *evidence mode*: give the user the read-only commands to run, and diagnose
    from the output, response bodies, and log entries they paste.
2.  **Authentication.** Use the user's existing `gcloud auth login` session;
    this skill doesn't need application-default credentials.
3.  **Project.** Ask which project hosts the gateway and pass
    `--project={project_id}` on every command. Don't run `gcloud config set`,
    because it changes the user's environment. This skill troubleshoots
    existing gateways and never creates projects.
4.  **Billing.** The project needs an active billing account even when usage
    stays in the free tier; see
    [API Gateway pricing](https://cloud.google.com/api-gateway/pricing).
5.  **APIs.** API Gateway requires `apigateway.googleapis.com`,
    `servicemanagement.googleapis.com`, and `servicecontrol.googleapis.com`. A
    gateway can keep responding while one of them is missing, and its logs then
    stay empty, so check with
    `gcloud services list --enabled --project={project_id}`. Enabling a missing
    API is a change that needs approval.
6.  **IAM roles for diagnosis (read-only):** `roles/apigateway.viewer`,
    `roles/logging.viewer`, `roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageViewer`, and
    `roles/iam.serviceAccountViewer` (to check the gateway's service account).
    For Cloud Run backends, add `roles/run.viewer`; to trace a custom domain
    through its load balancer, add `roles/compute.viewer`; to check an API key's
    project, `roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageViewer` is also needed there.
7.  **IAM roles for fixes (only after approval):** `roles/apigateway.admin`;
    `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` on the gateway's service account, because
    creating or updating an API config or a gateway requires
    `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs`;
    `roles/run.admin` to change a Cloud Run service's IAM policy or ingress;
    `roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin` to enable an API or a managed
    service, plus `roles/servicemanagement.serviceConsumer` on the API's
    managed service to enable it in another project; and
    `roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin` to re-enable a disabled service account.
8.  **Region.** Gateways are regional. Use the region that
    `gateways list` reports. When a fix needs a new gateway, create it in the
    original gateway's region, or in `us-central1` if the user has no
    preference; see
    [API Gateway deployment model](https://docs.cloud.google.com/api-gateway/docs/deployment-model.md.txt)
    and [Cloud locations](https://cloud.google.com/about/locations).

## Workflow

Copy this checklist into your notes and tick it off as you go:

```
- [ ] 1. Context collected
- [ ] 2. Gateway identified by defaultHostname
- [ ] 3. Expected or transient states ruled out
- [ ] 4. Gateway log entry read (bounded query)
- [ ] 5. One branch chosen from the classification table
- [ ] 6. Root cause stated with redacted evidence and a doc link
- [ ] 7. Fix proposed, approved, and applied (or handed to the user)
- [ ] 8. Fix verified
- [ ] 9. Escalated, if the evidence points to Google Cloud
```

### 1. Collect context

Extract these from the conversation first, and ask only for what's missing:

| Needed | Why |
| :--- | :--- |
| `{project_id}` of the gateway | Every command is scoped to it. |
| Failing URL (host and path) or `{gateway_id}` and `{region}` | Identifies the gateway. |
| HTTP method, status code, and response body | Separates gateway errors from backend errors. |
| Approximate time of the failure, in UTC | Bounds the log query. |
| What changed recently (new API config, IAM, backend deploy, DNS) | Recent changes are the first place to look. |
| Authentication used by the caller (API key, JWT, none) | Selects the auth branch. |

If the project or the host is unknown, stop and ask before you run any
`gcloud` command. Don't guess project IDs, and don't use the active `gcloud`
project instead.

### 2. Identify the gateway

List the project's gateways:

```bash
gcloud api-gateway gateways list --project={project_id} \
  --format="table(name.basename():label=GATEWAY,name.segment(3):label=REGION,defaultHostname,state,apiConfig)"
```

Match the request host against `defaultHostname`. Don't decide from the URL
suffix: a gateway's hostname can use either of two `gateway.dev` formats or,
for older streaming and model-routing gateways, a `run.app` format. Don't
guess the owning project from numbers in the hostname either; list the
gateways in the project the user names. A custom domain points at a load
balancer whose serverless NEG targets the gateway. See
[references/triage-and-logs.md](references/triage-and-logs.md) for the
hostname formats and how to trace a custom domain.

If no gateway in the project matches, confirm the product before going on
(see [Scope](#scope)).

Then read the gateway's details, including its API config and streaming mode:

```bash
gcloud api-gateway gateways describe {gateway_id} \
  --location={region} --project={project_id}
```

### 3. Rule out expected and transient states

-   **Gateway `state` isn't `ACTIVE`:** `CREATING` or `UPDATING` means an
    operation is still running, so wait and check again. `FAILED` means
    creation failed; read the error of the failed operation. `DELETING` means
    the gateway is being removed.
-   **API config just created:** creating a complex API config can take up to
    ten minutes, and only one config can be created for an API at a time.
-   **First requests after an idle period:** API Gateway has cold-start
    latency.
-   **Google Cloud incident:** check the
    [Service Health dashboard](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-health/docs/overview.md.txt).

### 4. Read the gateway log entry

Use a bounded query that prints only the fields you need. Replace
`{status_code}` with the status the caller saw:

```bash
gcloud logging read 'resource.type="apigateway.googleapis.com/Gateway" AND resource.labels.gateway_id="{gateway_id}" AND resource.labels.location="{region}" AND httpRequest.status={status_code}' \
  --project={project_id} --freshness=1h --limit=20 \
  --format="json(timestamp,httpRequest.status,httpRequest.latency,httpRequest.requestUrl,jsonPayload.responseDetails,jsonPayload.apiConfig,jsonPayload.apiMethod)"
```

If you know the failure time, replace `--freshness` with a
`timestamp>="{start_utc}" AND timestamp<="{end_utc}"` filter that spans about
30 minutes around it. Read `httpRequest.status`, `httpRequest.requestUrl`,
`jsonPayload.responseDetails`, `jsonPayload.apiConfig`, and
`jsonPayload.apiMethod`. Keep the `--format` field list, because a full entry
can contain the caller's credentials, and redact credentials before you quote
any field, including a `key` query parameter in `httpRequest.requestUrl`.

To compare API configs, compare only the `apis/{api_id}/configs/{config_id}`
part: the same config can appear as a full resource name
(`//apigateway.googleapis.com/projects/...`) and with either the project
number or the project ID.

`jsonPayload.responseDetails` decides the branch: `via_upstream` means the
backend produced the response; any other value means the gateway produced it.
The troubleshooting page explains `via_upstream` and
`service_control_quota_error`, and the model routing page explains the
`model_router_*` values that model-routing gateways log. Quote any other value
as-is, and don't explain how the gateway works internally.

### 5. Classify and follow one branch

Pick the first row that matches, and load only the reference file it names.

| What you see | Likely cause | Reference |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `401` or `403` with `via_upstream` | The backend rejected the gateway: invoker role, audience, or deleted service account | [auth-errors.md](references/auth-errors.md) |
| A `4xx` produced by the gateway whose body names a credential problem (for example `UNAUTHENTICATED`) | The API key or JWT was rejected; quote the body | [auth-errors.md](references/auth-errors.md) |
| `500` with **no** gateway log entry, after log exclusions and a wrong scope are ruled out | The gateway's service account may be deleted or disabled | [auth-errors.md](references/auth-errors.md) |
| `500` with `service_control_quota_error` | Quota metric missing from the newest API config | [config-deployment-errors.md](references/config-deployment-errors.md) |
| `429` with `service_control_quota_error` | The caller exceeded the API's quota | [limits-and-escalation.md](references/limits-and-escalation.md) |
| `404`, `502`, `503`, or `504`, an oversized request, or a timeout | Routing, backend errors, size limits, or the deadline. The docs don't name the status codes for size or deadline failures, so confirm with `responseDetails` and the body. | [backend-routing-and-timeouts.md](references/backend-routing-and-timeouts.md) |
| CORS preflight fails or latency is high | CORS pass-through or slow backend | [backend-routing-and-timeouts.md](references/backend-routing-and-timeouts.md) |
| `api-configs create` fails with an error about the OpenAPI document, such as an unsupported extension or an invalid path, parameter, server, or security requirement | A spec problem | Hand off to `api-gateway-openapi-spec-authoring`; if it isn't installed, see [OpenAPI pre-flight check](#openapi-pre-flight-check) |
| `api-configs create` fails with a service account, concurrency, or limit error, or `gateways create` or `gateways update` fails | Service account, concurrent creates, limits, or the backend deadline | [config-deployment-errors.md](references/config-deployment-errors.md) |
| `400` "The request was malformed" from an old TLS client, TLS scan findings, custom domain, or no log entry at all | TLS enforcement, DNS, load balancer, or wrong host | [networking-domains-tls.md](references/networking-domains-tls.md) |
| Errors on several gateways, or on an unchanged config, with healthy backends | Possible Google Cloud issue | [limits-and-escalation.md](references/limits-and-escalation.md) |

If the request also needs log queries or backend inspection commands, use
[triage-and-logs.md](references/triage-and-logs.md).

### 6. State the root cause

Give the cause, the evidence (redacted, quoted verbatim from logs or command
output), and the public doc section that explains it. If the evidence fits
more than one cause, list at most three, say what would tell them apart, and
collect that evidence before proposing a fix.

### 7. Propose the fix

Show the exact command, the resource it changes, its effect on live traffic,
and how to undo it. Wait for approval, then run it, or hand it to the user if
they prefer. Keep these rules in mind:

-   To change the OpenAPI document, create a new API config and deploy it with
    `gcloud api-gateway gateways update`. Before you create the config, check
    quota metrics with the `api-gateway-backend-security-and-rate-limiting`
    skill, because the newest API config's quota metrics apply to every
    gateway of the API.
-   Before you create a new API config, check the OpenAPI document with the
    linter (see [OpenAPI pre-flight check](#openapi-pre-flight-check)).

### 8. Verify

Read the logs again for new entries after the change, or repeat the failing
request. Repeat a request yourself only if it's safe to repeat, such as a
`GET`; otherwise ask the user to repeat it, because a repeated `POST` can
change data in their backend. After `gateways update`, wait until the
gateway's `state` is `ACTIVE` before you test.

### 9. Escalate when the evidence points to Google Cloud

Escalate to [Cloud Customer Care](https://cloud.google.com/support) when the
service account is active, the required APIs are enabled, and no log exclusion
or wrong scope explains it, but requests get `500` errors with no gateway log
entry; when several gateways fail at once without a config change; when errors
are intermittent on an unchanged config while the backend logs stay clean;
when control-plane operations keep failing with internal errors; or when
Service Health reports an incident. Draft the case text with the evidence
bundle in [limits-and-escalation.md](references/limits-and-escalation.md). The
user files the case.

## OpenAPI pre-flight check

Run the linter on every OpenAPI file before creating an API config. Run it;
don't read its source. If you don't have the file, give the user the command
to run:

```bash
python3 scripts/lint_openapi_for_gateway.py {spec_path} [{spec_path} ...]
```

It reads the files only, makes no network calls, and prints JSON findings that
each link to the public doc for the limitation. Exit code `0` means no errors,
`1` means at least one `ERROR` finding, and `2` means a usage, parse, or
dependency error. The linter needs Python 3.8 or later. YAML input needs
PyYAML; ask the user before you install it with
`pip install "PyYAML>=6.0,<7.0"`. JSON input doesn't. Fix the `ERROR`
findings, and then create the API config. If `api-configs create` still fails
on the OpenAPI document, hand off to `api-gateway-openapi-spec-authoring`, or
use the error message if that skill isn't installed. Show `WARNING` findings
to the user and explain them.

## Output format

Report findings in this form:

```
**Problem:** <one sentence in the user's terms>
**Failed hop:** <gateway or backend, and the evidence for it>
**Evidence:** <redacted log fields or command output, verbatim>
**Root cause:** <one or two sentences> (<public doc link>)
**Fix:** <exact command or spec change; approval needed: yes/no>
**Verify:** <how to confirm the fix>
**Open questions:** <anything you couldn't confirm>
```

# Apigee as an Agent Gateway Service Extension

Wires an Apigee proxy in as an **ext-proc callout** on a GCP Agent Gateway. The
proxy is a **processor, not an API proxy**: it has no backend, inspects the LLM
request and response the gateway hands it, and returns a verdict.

## Usage Attribution

**MUST READ**: Before executing any `gcloud`, REST API, or MCP command, you
MUST read and follow the instructions in
[Usage Attribution](references/attribution.md).

You build the proxy; the user does not.

**Two modes, one schema. Decide which before anything else, and say which.**
Input file present → **prod mode**: it is the contract, every value comes from
it, and a missing or malformed field is a refusal, not a default. No input file
and the user is describing an outcome → **dev mode**: apply the documented
defaults, show a plan with durations and get approval, start with identity and
metering only, write `apigee-agent-gateway-governance.yaml` at the end as the
handoff. `assets/apigee-agent-gateway-governance.example.yaml` documents the
schema both modes use.

Modes, defaults, durations, cost disclosure and the interlocks that bind both:
`references/modes.md`. **Read it before you start.**

**Colour the plan's ACTION column** — green `REUSE`, cyan `CREATE`/`RESERVE`,
yellow `APPEND`/`MODIFY`; full palette in `references/modes.md`. Yellow is the
one that earns its place: it is the only signal that a resource the user already
owns is being changed. Rendered plain, the one row that modifies something is
indistinguishable from the dozen that do not — which is exactly the row the
approval exists for.

## Prerequisite: where the agent runs

Check this **before** building anything. It decides whether traffic can reach
the gateway at all, and it is silent when wrong — every step below still
succeeds while nothing arrives.

**Use Agent Runtime**, created with `agent_gateway_config` /
`agent_to_anywhere_config`. It is the supported path and the orchestrator builds
the client-side PSC, routing, DNS and cert trust for you. There is no `gcloud`
surface for this and no console path — it is SDK-only, at agent creation time.
See
[Route traffic through Agent Gateway](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/scale/runtime/agent-gateway-runtime-deploy.md.txt)
for the binding, and `references/networking-psc.md` for a worked example.

**Set `GOOGLE_API_PREVENT_AGENT_TOKEN_SHARING_FOR_GCP_SERVICES: "False"` in the
agent's `env_vars`, or every invocation 401s** on the agent's own
`sessions.create`, before user code runs. Deploy-time invisible. Full symptom
and isolation: `references/gotchas.md`, Agent Gateway.

Where the agent runs is otherwise settled — the premise is a working gateway and
a working agent. Do not explain how to build one or list unsupported compute
unprompted; `references/networking-psc.md` has the constraints if it turns out
to matter.

## Tool versions

Do not assume these are installed or current.

Tool                                         | Minimum     | Why
-------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ---
`gcloud`                                     | **588.0.0** | `apigee apis import --from-template` is on the GA track at this version; older SDKs need `gcloud beta`
`google-cloud-aiplatform[agent_engines,adk]` | `>=2.1,<3`  | Agent Runtime client used to bind the agent to the gateway
`google-adk`                                 | `>=2.9,<3`  | only if you build the test agent with ADK

**On gcloud >= 588.0.0: every feature must keep its `uid`, and the template must
never declare `endpoints` or `targets`.** All six features set `uid` today and
the template declares neither, so the shipped bundle is correct — but both are
load-bearing now, and breaking either one still compiles, still deploys, and
reports nothing. Mechanism and symptoms: `references/gotchas.md`, under
Authoring (AFT).

```bash
gcloud version | head -1          # confirm >= 588.0.0
gcloud components update          # if older
pip install "google-cloud-aiplatform[agent_engines,adk]>=2.1,<3" "google-adk>=2.9,<3"
```

`scripts/compile_check.py` needs PyYAML and names the interpreter if it is
missing. `pip install pyyaml`, or run it with a Python 3 that has it; gcloud's
bundled interpreter does not, and the SDK's vendored `yaml` is Python 2.

```bash
python3 scripts/compile_check.py assets/apigee-proxy-template.yaml
```

## Execution model

Three layers, and the choice between them is not stylistic:

Layer                 | Used for                                               | Why
--------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ---
**AFT YAML template** | the proxy itself                                       | version-controlled, reviewable, diffable
**`gcloud`**          | PSC, DNS, AuthzExtension, AuthzPolicy                  | native commands exist
**REST (`curl`)**     | env properties, envgroups, deployments, debug sessions | no `gcloud` equivalent today

The customer owns **one** input file
(`assets/apigee-agent-gateway-governance.example.yaml`). It is the
version-controlled artifact. Never hand-edit the generated proxy: regenerate it.

**Run the Apigee-side sequence with the script, not by hand.** Steps 1, 3 and 4
below are order-dependent and each fails in a way that reads as a different
problem. `scripts/deploy_proxy.sh` does all three, preserves the properties
map, polls the async operation, and exits non-zero if the deployment does not
come up `EXTENSIBLE`:

```bash
scripts/deploy_proxy.sh --org "$ORG" --env "$ENV" --proxy "$PROXY" \
  --template assets/apigee-proxy-template.yaml [--service-account "$SA"] --yes \
  [--index-endpoint-id ID --index-id ID --sc-project P --sc-region R --embeddings-model M]
```

Run it without `--yes` first: it prints the plan and changes nothing. Show that
plan, then re-run with `--yes` once the user agrees.

**The vector-search flags are the one exception to "edit the default in every
feature that declares it".** Those three ids are substituted at deploy time
and checked for leftovers; hand-editing them into `feature-semantic-cache.yaml`
deploys fine, skips the check, and makes the file single-use.

`scripts/ensure_gateway_connectivity.sh` is the same idea for the gateway leg
(step 0). It is the only part of this skill that modifies a resource the user
already owns, so it applies nothing without `--yes`.

The steps are written out below so you can diagnose a failure, not so you can
retype them.

## Inputs you must resolve first

**Environment prerequisites: `references/setup.md`** — gcloud SDK (588+),
project, billing, `gcloud services enable`, region, credentials, IAM. Nothing
below creates any of it.

Prod: from the input file, then environment, then ask — never invent. Dev: apply
the `references/modes.md` defaults, and ask only for what has none.

-   `project`, `region`
-   `apigee.org`, `apigee.environment`, `apigee.envgroup`, `apigee.hostname`,
    `apigee.proxy`
-   `network.vpc`, `network.subnet`, `network.networkAttachment`
-   `gateway.name`, `gateway.matchPaths` (a **list**, one entry per wire shape),
    `gateway.manageNetworkConfig`

**`matchPaths` drives TWO artifacts; write both from the same list.** The
**AuthzPolicy** `paths[].suffix` gets one suffix per entry, verbatim with
leading punctuation kept — it decides what the gateway routes to Apigee. The
template's **`LLM_URI_MATCH`** gets one `(request.uri Like "*<entry>*")` clause
per entry, OR-ed, leading `:` or `/` **stripped** — it decides what the proxy
acts on once it arrives. The shipped two-entry default gives:

```
((request.uri Like "*generateContent*") or (request.uri Like "*chat/completions*"))
```

The AuthzPolicy is the outer gate and wins: a suffix list narrower than
`matchPaths` means the missing shape never reaches Apigee at all. Derive both
from the input file and never from the default when the file disagrees — the
file is the reviewable contract and a mismatch is invisible once deployed.

**A one-entry list is legitimate** and governs one shape. Dropping an entry
governs one fewer **silently** — deploys clean, zero transactions for the shape
dropped — and narrows `feature-normalize`, Model Armor and the cache together.
`references/gotchas.md`, Runtime.

**`semanticCache` is a KNOWN ISSUE whenever it is on — warn, then build it.**
The key is the prompt embedding alone: no caller, no model, no shape. A hit
therefore crosses callers — similar prompts share an answer — and one model
behind one shape does not make it safe. With more shapes the first model to
answer answers for the other too: empty HTTP 200 across shapes, wrong-model
body within one. Warn whenever the cache is on, not only on multi-shape, then

cannot resolve the callout hostname. **This skill builds it** — network
attachment, egress and DNS peering — so its absence is a build step, not a
blocker, and should be reported that way. Do not open with an alarm about a
resource you are about to create.

than a silent prerequisite: attaching egress is **one-way and affects traffic
they already run**. Settle it in the plan, before anything executes — see
"Confirm everything up front" below. Capturing a known-good agent turn first is
worth doing when they are nervous about a production gateway, because it
separates "never worked" from "we broke it"; it is a precaution to offer, not a
step to impose.

```bash

  --location="$REGION" --project="$PROJECT" --format='value(networkConfig)'

  --location="$REGION" --project="$PROJECT"
```

**A console-created gateway already has a CUSTOM AuthzPolicy** — an IAP
`REQUEST_AUTHZ` one, which coexists with ours and is not needed for the egress
JWT. You never create the gateway, so assess it rather than assuming.

-   **`false`** — the user has said they want to make this change themselves.

```bash
  --gateway "$GATEWAY" --project "$PROJECT" --region "$REGION" \
  --vpc "$VPC" --subnet "$SUBNET" --attachment "$ATTACHMENT" \
```

because its absence is an error, but because every later step then succeeds and
governs nothing.

hand-built YAML silently drops the gateway's `registries` and `protocols`. Why,

exists; PATCH the properties map.

```bash
  "https://apigee.googleapis.com/v1/organizations/$ORG/environments/$ENV"
```

you intend to keep, or you will silently drop them.

```bash
curl -X PATCH -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  "https://apigee.googleapis.com/v1/organizations/$ORG/environments/$ENV?updateMask=properties" \
  -d '{"properties":{"property":[{"name":"apigee-service-extension-enabled","value":"true"}]}}'
```

missing it is the separate per-environment add-on. `references/gotchas.md`.

environment in two makes the gateway 404 every request with the extension never
invoked. It also leaves the `/` base path free, which is what the proxy ships
with.

nothing without `--yes`; that agreement is taken in the plan, not here.

```bash
  --org "$ORG" --env "$ENV" --region "$REGION" \
  --envgroup "$ENVGROUP" --hostname "$HOSTNAME"      # add --yes to apply
```

already in another envgroup or the envgroup exists on a different hostname. It
also handles three things a runbook tends to get wrong — the omitted `type` on

polling the operation rather than a `GET` that succeeds too early.

Done already if step 1's script ran. Verify, or do it by hand for an envgroup
that already exists. The hostname must be exactly the callout host, and the
group must be attached to the env.

```bash

  "https://apigee.googleapis.com/v1/organizations/$ORG/envgroups/$ENVGROUP/attachments"
```

never lands. `deploy_proxy.sh` enforces this before touching anything and exits

it fires — the environment is wrong, not the script.

### 3. Build the proxy from the template

```bash
gcloud apigee apis import organizations/$ORG/apis/$PROXY \
  --from-template=assets/apigee-proxy-template.yaml
```

directory**, never the working directory, so a bare filename must sit beside the
template (a subpath like `features/feature-identity.yaml` works too). `assets/`
is flat by convention, not compiler demand — but moving a file without updating

you demonstrably have access to, it is the credential, not the access. With
context-aware access enabled the default gcloud credential is rejected. Pass the
ADC token instead:

```bash
CLOUDSDK_AUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN=$(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token) \
  gcloud apigee apis import ...
```

— not in the template. `gcloud apigee apis import` passes an empty
caller-parameter map, so each feature resolves its own default and the
template's declaration of the same name is never read. Editing the template
changes nothing, silently, and the compile still passes. Measured: setting

fail-closed policy. `LLM_URI_MATCH` is declared in four features and all four
must agree. `scripts/compile_check.py` fails on any disagreement. There is no
`--parameters` flag.

Enable an optional recipe by adding its feature to the template's `features`
list. See `references/recipes.md`.

which buckets exist; it does not create them. A bucket is real only when it has

**omitting `other`
silently unmeters every non-Gemini model**: the count is extracted and then
discarded, with no `ratelimit` reference anywhere in the transaction. Adding a
model is a feature-file edit, not a config change.

```bash

```

The **agent → gateway** leg is the prerequisite above, and is not built here.

that **breaks the agent's turn**. Historically the most common failure here.

does not fire. Broaden the policy and it fires at once: the ext-proc then sees
every agent egress — session create/read, `appendEvent`, OpenTelemetry exports —

call. Gate the steps regardless; a condition is cheap and it is what makes the
policy safe to widen later. Full measurement: `references/gotchas.md`.

**Never fail-close on your own metering.** Keep `continueOnError="true"` on the
JavaScript and quota policies so a metering bug cannot break LLM traffic.

**This skill meters by default and can enforce on request.** Enforcement is
`assets/feature-token-enforce.yaml`: request-flow `EnforceOnly` policies sharing
each `SharedName` with the response-flow `CountOnly` half. Add it to the
template's feature list. Verified live on ext-proc traffic — the over-budget
caller gets a **429**, model never called.

gate (the answer is already on the wire) and it freezes the counter, losing the
metering too.

that crosses the limit completes, because a token cost is not known until the
model answers. And it buckets on the **requested** model, which under an OpenAI
alias can differ from the resolved model the counting side bills. The two traps
that both present as "it never refuses": `references/gotchas.md`.

model is an alias in the request body and the *resolved* name is in the response
body (`google/gemini-4-argon`). Exact-matching a raw name fails on the response
path.

**`jsonPath` needs its third argument `true`** so it returns a scalar. Without
it the quota policy receives a node it cannot parse.

# Apigee as an Agent Gateway Service Extension

Wires an Apigee proxy in as an **ext-proc callout** on a GCP Agent Gateway. The
proxy is a **processor, not an API proxy**: it has no backend, inspects the LLM
request and response the gateway hands it, and returns a verdict.

## Usage Attribution

**MUST READ**: Before executing any `gcloud`, REST API, or MCP command, you
MUST read and follow the instructions in
[Usage Attribution](references/attribution.md).

You build the proxy; the user does not.

**Two modes, one schema. Decide which before anything else, and say which.**
Input file present → **prod mode**: it is the contract, every value comes from
it, and a missing or malformed field is a refusal, not a default. No input file
and the user is describing an outcome → **dev mode**: apply the documented
defaults, show a plan with durations and get approval, start with identity and
metering only, write `apigee-agent-gateway-governance.yaml` at the end as the
handoff. `assets/apigee-agent-gateway-governance.example.yaml` documents the
schema both modes use.

Modes, defaults, durations, cost disclosure and the interlocks that bind both:
`references/modes.md`. **Read it before you start.**

**Colour the plan's ACTION column** — green `REUSE`, cyan `CREATE`/`RESERVE`,
yellow `APPEND`/`MODIFY`; full palette in `references/modes.md`. Yellow is the
one that earns its place: it is the only signal that a resource the user already
owns is being changed. Rendered plain, the one row that modifies something is
indistinguishable from the dozen that do not — which is exactly the row the
approval exists for.

## Prerequisite: where the agent runs

Check this **before** building anything. It decides whether traffic can reach
the gateway at all, and it is silent when wrong — every step below still
succeeds while nothing arrives.

**Use Agent Runtime**, created with `agent_gateway_config` /
`agent_to_anywhere_config`. It is the supported path and the orchestrator builds
the client-side PSC, routing, DNS and cert trust for you. There is no `gcloud`
surface for this and no console path — it is SDK-only, at agent creation time.
See
[Route traffic through Agent Gateway](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/scale/runtime/agent-gateway-runtime-deploy.md.txt)
for the binding, and `references/networking-psc.md` for a worked example.

**Set `GOOGLE_API_PREVENT_AGENT_TOKEN_SHARING_FOR_GCP_SERVICES: "False"` in the
agent's `env_vars`, or every invocation 401s** on the agent's own
`sessions.create`, before user code runs. Deploy-time invisible. Full symptom
and isolation: `references/gotchas.md`, Agent Gateway.

Where the agent runs is otherwise settled — the premise is a working gateway and
a working agent. Do not explain how to build one or list unsupported compute
unprompted; `references/networking-psc.md` has the constraints if it turns out
to matter.

## Tool versions

Do not assume these are installed or current.

Tool                                         | Minimum     | Why
-------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ---
`gcloud`                                     | **588.0.0** | `apigee apis import --from-template` is on the GA track at this version; older SDKs need `gcloud beta`
`google-cloud-aiplatform[agent_engines,adk]` | `>=2.1,<3`  | Agent Runtime client used to bind the agent to the gateway
`google-adk`                                 | `>=2.9,<3`  | only if you build the test agent with ADK

**On gcloud >= 588.0.0: every feature must keep its `uid`, and the template must
never declare `endpoints` or `targets`.** All six features set `uid` today and
the template declares neither, so the shipped bundle is correct — but both are
load-bearing now, and breaking either one still compiles, still deploys, and
reports nothing. Mechanism and symptoms: `references/gotchas.md`, under
Authoring (AFT).

```bash
gcloud version | head -1          # confirm >= 588.0.0
gcloud components update          # if older
pip install "google-cloud-aiplatform[agent_engines,adk]>=2.1,<3" "google-adk>=2.9,<3"
```

`scripts/compile_check.py` needs PyYAML and names the interpreter if it is
missing. `pip install pyyaml`, or run it with a Python 3 that has it; gcloud's
bundled interpreter does not, and the SDK's vendored `yaml` is Python 2.

```bash
python3 scripts/compile_check.py assets/apigee-proxy-template.yaml
```

## Execution model

Three layers, and the choice between them is not stylistic:

Layer                 | Used for                                               | Why
--------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ---
**AFT YAML template** | the proxy itself                                       | version-controlled, reviewable, diffable
**`gcloud`**          | PSC, DNS, AuthzExtension, AuthzPolicy                  | native commands exist
**REST (`curl`)**     | env properties, envgroups, deployments, debug sessions | no `gcloud` equivalent today

The customer owns **one** input file
(`assets/apigee-agent-gateway-governance.example.yaml`). It is the
version-controlled artifact. Never hand-edit the generated proxy: regenerate it.

```bash
  --envgroup "$ENVGROUP" --hostname "$HOSTNAME"      # add --yes to apply
```

It is idempotent and resumable, and refuses with exit 2 when the environment is
already in another envgroup or the envgroup exists on a different hostname. It
also handles three things a runbook tends to get wrong — the omitted `type` on
create, the four-minute instance attachment that **locks the environment**, and
polling the operation rather than a `GET` that succeeds too early.

### 2. Apigee: envgroup on the callout hostname

Done already if step 1's script ran. Verify, or do it by hand for an envgroup
that already exists. The hostname must be exactly the callout host, and the
group must be attached to the env.

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://apigee.googleapis.com/v1/organizations/$ORG/envgroups/$ENVGROUP/attachments"
```

**How many envgroups is the environment in?** More than one and the callout
never lands. `deploy_proxy.sh` enforces this before touching anything and exits
2 naming them; `assess_integration.sh` reports it. Read the failure literally if
it fires — the environment is wrong, not the script.

### 3. Build the proxy from the template

```bash
gcloud apigee apis import organizations/$ORG/apis/$PROXY \
  --from-template=assets/apigee-proxy-template.yaml
```

Each `features:` entry resolves **relative to the template file's own
directory**, never the working directory, so a bare filename must sit beside the
template (a subpath like `features/feature-identity.yaml` works too). `assets/`
is flat by convention, not compiler demand — but moving a file without updating
`features:` fails the import with a bare `FileNotFoundError`.

If you get `Permission denied on resource ... (or it may not exist)` on an org
you demonstrably have access to, it is the credential, not the access. With
context-aware access enabled the default gcloud credential is rejected. Pass the
ADC token instead:

```bash
CLOUDSDK_AUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN=$(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token) \
  gcloud apigee apis import ...
```

To change a parameter, **edit the `default` in every FEATURE that declares it**
— not in the template. `gcloud apigee apis import` passes an empty
caller-parameter map, so each feature resolves its own default and the
template's declaration of the same name is never read. Editing the template
changes nothing, silently, and the compile still passes. Measured: setting
`MA_CONTINUE_ON_ERROR` to DRY_RUN in the template shipped ENFORCE on a
fail-closed policy. `LLM_URI_MATCH` is declared in four features and all four
must agree. `scripts/compile_check.py` fails on any disagreement. There is no
`--parameters` flag.

Enable an optional recipe by adding its feature to the template's `features`
list. See `references/recipes.md`.

**`tokenMetering.models` in the input file is NOT generative.** It documents
which buckets exist; it does not create them. A bucket is real only when it has
an `LLMTokenQuota` step in `feature-token-metering.yaml` and a matching
`*_TOKEN_LIMIT` parameter. Three exist: `gemini-pro`, `gemini-flash` and `other`
— the catch-all for any model whose name contains neither `pro`/`argon` nor
`flash`/`hydrogen`. Adding a fourth entry to the list meters nothing, and
**omitting `other`
silently unmeters every non-Gemini model**: the count is extracted and then
discarded, with no `ratelimit` reference anywhere in the transaction. Adding a
model is a feature-file edit, not a config change.

### 4. Deploy

Deploy to the service-extension env, then confirm the deployment reports
`proxyDeploymentType: EXTENSIBLE`.

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  ".../environments/$ENV/deployments"
```

`STANDARD` means it will **not** govern the agent's off-Apigee tool egress.

If any policy calls a Google API — Model Armor, embeddings, Vector Search —
deploy **with a service account** or the deploy is rejected with
`MISSING_SERVICE_ACCOUNT`:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  ".../apis/$PROXY/revisions/$REV/deployments?override=true&serviceAccount=$DEPLOY_SA"
```

### 5. Networking

This is the **gateway → Apigee** leg only. PSC endpoint to the Apigee instance
service attachment, plus a private DNS A record. See
`references/networking-psc.md`. The Apigee instance `consumerAcceptList` must
include your project or the connection never reaches `ACCEPTED`.

The **agent → gateway** leg is the prerequisite above, and is not built here.

### 6. Bind the gateway

AuthzExtension then AuthzPolicy — in that order, and only once the host resolves
and the proxy is deployed. The extension is inert until then.

**Both document bodies ship as assets. Copy and substitute; do not invent them**
— `assets/authz-extension.example.yaml` and `assets/authz-policy.example.yaml`.
They carry the fields that are load-bearing and have no obvious default:
`wireFormat: EXT_PROC_GRPC`, `failOpen`, the `authority`/`service` pair, the
`metadata` body flags, and the policy's `customProvider` / `httpRules` nesting.

```bash
gcloud service-extensions authz-extensions import $AUTHZ_EXT \
  --source=authz-extension.yaml --location=$REGION --project=$PROJECT
gcloud beta network-security authz-policies import $AUTHZ_POLICY \
  --source=authz-policy.yaml --location=$REGION --project=$PROJECT
```

**The policy's resource paths take the project NUMBER, not the ID** — both
`target.resources` and `customProvider.authzExtension.resources`. Resolve it
yourself; narrating two numbers at the user does not help. The trap, for when a
callout never lands: the number in the gateway's
`serviceExtensionsServiceAccount` is the Google-managed tenant project, not
theirs, and it is the only one on screen, so it is the natural thing to copy. A
wrong number imports cleanly and targets nothing. Copy the slots from
`assets/authz-policy.example.yaml`.

### 7. Verify

You **cannot** test with curl — the host is internal and the proxy expects the
gateway's IAP-egress JWT. Run `scripts/read_debug_session.sh --arm`, drive a
turn, read it back with `--session`. Expect **one** transaction per turn per
governed shape under a suffix list this narrow; zero alone does not mean the
callout is dead — the script prints the probe that settles it.

## Hard rules

**Gate every step — how urgently depends on your AuthzPolicy.** An ungated
`continueOnError="false"` policy faults on any call that carries no prompt, and
that **breaks the agent's turn**. Historically the most common failure here.

A narrow suffix list routes only the model call to Apigee, so the trap mostly
does not fire. Broaden the policy and it fires at once: the ext-proc then sees
every agent egress — session create/read, `appendEvent`, OpenTelemetry exports —
measured at 12 calls for one single-question turn, of which one was the model
call. Gate the steps regardless; a condition is cheap and it is what makes the
policy safe to widen later. Full measurement: `references/gotchas.md`.

-   model call: `(request.uri Like "*generateContent*")`

**Never fail-close on your own metering.** Keep `continueOnError="true"` on the
JavaScript and quota policies so a metering bug cannot break LLM traffic.

**This skill meters by default and can enforce on request.** Enforcement is
`assets/feature-token-enforce.yaml`: request-flow `EnforceOnly` policies sharing
each `SharedName` with the response-flow `CountOnly` half. Add it to the
template's feature list. Verified live on ext-proc traffic — the over-budget
caller gets a **429**, model never called.

Never offer `CountOnly=false` as a substitute: in the response flow it cannot
gate (the answer is already on the wire) and it freezes the counter, losing the
metering too.

State two things whenever you offer it. It is **one request late** — the turn
that crosses the limit completes, because a token cost is not known until the
model answers. And it buckets on the **requested** model, which under an OpenAI
alias can differ from the resolved model the counting side bills. The two traps
that both present as "it never refuses": `references/gotchas.md`.

**Normalize the model to a bucket.** With an OpenAI-compatible endpoint the
model is an alias in the request body and the *resolved* name is in the response
body (`google/gemini-4-argon`). Exact-matching a raw name fails on the response
path.

**`jsonPath` needs its third argument `true`** so it returns a scalar. Without
it the quota policy receives a node it cannot parse.

description: >-
